mcqs.question: Why were lambdas added to Java in version 8 rather than Java always having had them?
options: Functions were not first-class values before then, so passing behavior meant passing an object with one method instead of a function value directly
Java could not run loops efficiently before Java 8
Lambdas were added purely to shorten syntax; functions were already first-class
Java needed lambdas to support garbage collection of closures
mcqs.explanation: Before Java 8, a function couldn't be passed as a value — you passed an object implementing a single-method interface instead, which is functionally similar but syntactically and conceptually heavier. Lambdas made functions first-class; this had nothing to do with loop performance or garbage collection.

mcqs.question: Which of map, filter, and reduce is the most general, in the sense that the other two can be expressed using it?
options: map, because it can produce any output filter or reduce could
filter, because it's the only one that can skip elements
None of them — the three are independent primitives with no overlap
reduce, because folding a collection into an accumulator can express both keeping elements and transforming them
mcqs.explanation: reduce is the most general: you can implement map by folding each element's transformed result into a growing list, and filter by folding only elements that pass the predicate into the accumulator. map and filter are convenient special cases, not independent primitives.

mcqs.question: An imperative loop computes a running total while also filtering out rows with a condition, all in one loop body. Which functional shape does this map onto?
options: A single map call, since the loop only transforms values
A filter followed by a reduce — keep the rows that pass the condition, then fold them into a total
A single filter call, since the loop's only job is dropping rows
Currying, since the loop combines two operations into one
mcqs.explanation: The condition that decides whether a row counts is a filter, and accumulating a running total is exactly what reduce does — the pattern is filter-then-reduce. There's no transformation of individual values here, so plain map doesn't fit, and currying is about argument application, unrelated to this loop shape.

mcqs.question: What's the precise difference between currying and partial application?
options: There is no difference; the two terms describe identical behavior in every language
Partial application only works in statically typed languages, while currying only works in dynamically typed ones
Currying transforms a function into a chain of one-argument functions; partial application is the broader idea of fixing some arguments now and waiting for the rest, in any calling convention
Currying fixes some arguments and returns a value immediately; partial application always returns another function
mcqs.explanation: Currying is specifically about restructuring a function into a unary chain (f(a)(b)(c)); partial application is more general and doesn't require that restructuring — Python's functools.partial fixes arguments without true currying. Neither is tied to a typing discipline, and the third option reverses the roles.

mcqs.question: You need to add exactly one more filtering step to an existing three-stage map/filter/reduce pipeline. What does that typically require compared to doing the same to a single imperative loop body?
options: It's usually simpler — insert one more filter call into the chain, without touching the existing stages' logic
It's strictly harder, because pipelines can't be extended without rewriting every stage
It's about the same effort either way — both require touching the same number of lines
It requires rewriting the reduce step, since filter and reduce are tightly coupled
mcqs.explanation: A named-stage pipeline lets you insert a new stage without editing the logic of existing ones, whereas an imperative loop body often requires threading a new condition through existing mutable state and control flow. Pipelines are not harder to extend, and filter/reduce aren't coupled such that one requires rewriting the other.

mcqs.question: A deeply composed pipeline (compose(f, compose(g, h))) throws an exception, and the stack trace shows only the composition machinery, not which named function actually failed. What's the recommended fix from this slide?
options: Stop using composition entirely and rewrite everything as loops
Prefer a pipe-style chain over deep nested composition, or temporarily name intermediate results so a debugger can step through each stage
Wrap the whole pipeline in a single generic try/except that swallows the error
Ignore it — composed pipelines are expected to be undebuggable by design
mcqs.explanation: The fix targets debuggability without giving up composition: pipe-style chains or named intermediates let you inspect the value between stages. Abandoning composition altogether or swallowing the exception both throw away the benefit instead of addressing the actual debugging gap.
